questions.title: A highly cellular cerebellar tumour with Homer Wright rosettes, WHO Grade IV and radiosensitive — what is it?
questions.question: A child presents with a cerebellar tumour. Histological examination reveals a highly cellular tumour with anaplasia, mitoses and Homer Wright rosettes. The tumour is classified as WHO Grade IV and is radiosensitive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hemangioblastoma is a benign (WHO Grade I), slow-growing, highly vascular tumour composed of vacuolated stromal cells and thin-walled vessels — it does not show anaplasia, brisk mitoses or Homer Wright rosettes, and is not WHO Grade IV.
explanations.B: Correct. This combination — a highly cellular small round blue cell tumour with anaplasia, mitotic activity and Homer Wright rosettes, graded WHO Grade IV yet radiosensitive — is the classic description of medulloblastoma, the most common malignant cerebellar tumour of childhood. It typically arises in the cerebellar vermis and can seed the cerebrospinal fluid, so staging includes imaging of the whole neuraxis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign (WHO Grade I) cerebellar tumour of childhood with Rosenthal fibres and biphasic architecture, not the anaplastic, rosette-forming, WHO Grade IV picture described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ependymoma arises from ependymal cells lining the ventricles and shows perivascular pseudorosettes (and true ependymal rosettes), a different histological pattern from the Homer Wright rosettes of medulloblastoma.

questions.learning_objective: Identify medulloblastoma from the combination of Homer Wright rosettes, anaplasia/mitoses, WHO Grade IV grading and radiosensitivity.

questions.title: A slow-growing, benign, highly vascular cerebellar tumour with vacuolated cells and thin-walled vessels — what is it?
questions.question: A patient presents with a slow-growing, benign, highly vascular cerebellar tumour. Histologically, it is composed of large vacuolated cells and thin-walled vessels. This tumour is most likely a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medulloblastoma is a malignant, WHO Grade IV, highly cellular small round blue cell tumour — the opposite of the benign, slow-growing, vacuolated-cell picture described here.
explanations.B: Correct. Large, lipid-vacuolated ("foamy") stromal cells amid a dense network of thin-walled capillary-sized vessels is the classic histology of hemangioblastoma, a benign (WHO Grade I), highly vascular cerebellar tumour often associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. The stromal cells are considered the true neoplastic element, with the rich vasculature a secondary proliferation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metastatic clear cell (renal cell) carcinoma can mimic hemangioblastoma's vacuolated cells, but it is a malignant metastatic lesion, not the benign, slow-growing tumour described, and typically shows more nuclear atypia and a history of a primary renal tumour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pilocytic astrocytoma is benign and can be cystic and vascular, but its histology is defined by biphasic architecture and Rosenthal fibres, not large vacuolated stromal cells with thin-walled vessels.

questions.learning_objective: State that hemangioblastoma's histology shows large vacuolated stromal cells amid thin-walled capillary channels.

questions.title: Which genetic abnormality is most commonly associated with medulloblastoma?
questions.question: What is the genetic abnormality most commonly associated with the WHO integrated diagnosis of medulloblastoma?

options.A: Loss of chromosome 17p and duplication of 17q (isochromosome 17q)

explanations.A: Correct. Isochromosome 17q — loss of 17p (which carries the TP53 locus) with duplication of 17q — is the single most common cytogenetic abnormality found in medulloblastoma, distinct from the newer molecular-subtype markers (WNT/SHH/Group 3/Group 4) used alongside it in the integrated diagnosis. It is a karyotypic finding that can be identified across multiple molecular subtypes rather than defining one subtype specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. EGFR amplification is a hallmark of glioblastoma, a supratentorial adult glioma, not medulloblastoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1p/19q co-deletion is the defining molecular marker of oligodendroglioma, an adult supratentorial glioma, not medulloblastoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. IDH1 mutation characterises diffuse (lower-grade) adult gliomas and secondary glioblastoma, not the embryonal tumour medulloblastoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that isochromosome 17q is the genetic abnormality most commonly associated with medulloblastoma.

questions.title: Nuclear beta-catenin positivity in medulloblastoma is most characteristic of which molecular subtype?
questions.question: A patient is diagnosed with a cerebellar medulloblastoma. Immunohistochemistry reveals nuclear beta-catenin positivity. This finding is most characteristic of which molecular subtype?

explanations.A: Correct. Nuclear (rather than membranous or cytoplasmic) beta-catenin immunopositivity reflects constitutive activation of the Wnt signalling pathway and is the immunohistochemical hallmark of the WNT-activated molecular subtype of medulloblastoma, which also carries the most favourable prognosis of the four subtypes. This subtype is also enriched for germline or somatic CTNNB1 and APC pathway alterations.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The SHH-activated subtype is instead marked by GAB1 and/or YAP1 immunopositivity, reflecting activation of the Sonic Hedgehog pathway, not nuclear beta-catenin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Group 3 medulloblastoma, often associated with MYC amplification and a poor prognosis, is not defined by nuclear beta-catenin positivity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Group 4 medulloblastoma, the most common subtype overall, is not defined by nuclear beta-catenin positivity either; it is currently identified largely by exclusion of the other three subtypes plus supporting molecular markers.

questions.learning_objective: Identify nuclear beta-catenin positivity as diagnostic of the WNT-activated molecular subtype of medulloblastoma.

questions.title: A well-circumscribed reddish vermian mass bulging into the fourth ventricle — what is it?
questions.question: A patient presents with a cerebellar tumour. The tumour is slow-growing, well-circumscribed and located in the vermis, bulging into the fourth ventricle. Grossly, it is a reddish mass. This is most consistent with a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medulloblastoma is a malignant, infiltrative tumour of childhood, not the well-circumscribed, slow-growing, reddish mass described, which reflects a benign, highly vascular lesion.
explanations.B: Correct. A well-circumscribed, slow-growing, reddish (highly vascular) vermian mass bulging into the fourth ventricle is the classic gross description of hemangioblastoma, whose colour reflects its dense capillary network. Larger tumours in this location can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and produce obstructive hydrocephalus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metastatic melanoma can occasionally be pigmented or haemorrhagic, but it is typically an ill-defined, multifocal, infiltrative lesion in a patient with a known primary, not a solitary well-circumscribed vermian mass.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pilocytic astrocytoma is typically a cystic, greyish-tan mass with a mural nodule, not the solid reddish mass described here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the gross appearance of hemangioblastoma as a well-circumscribed reddish vermian mass bulging into the fourth ventricle.

questions.title: What does a WHO Grade IV classification of medulloblastoma indicate?
questions.question: A young child is diagnosed with medulloblastoma. The tumour is classified as WHO Grade IV. This grading indicates that the tumour is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. WHO Grade I, not Grade IV, denotes a benign, slow-growing tumour (as in pilocytic astrocytoma or hemangioblastoma).
explanations.B: Correct. The WHO CNS tumour grading scale runs from Grade I (benign) to Grade IV (malignant, rapidly proliferating and prone to craniospinal dissemination); medulloblastoma's Grade IV designation reflects this malignant, highly aggressive behaviour. Despite this, its notable radiosensitivity makes adjuvant radiotherapy an effective part of treatment after surgery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Grade IV tumours are typically infiltrative/invasive and prone to spread, not non-invasive.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Higher WHO grade generally correlates with poorer differentiation (more anaplasia), not with being well-differentiated.

questions.learning_objective: State that medulloblastoma's WHO Grade IV designation reflects malignant, highly aggressive tumour behaviour.

questions.title: What percentage of childhood brain tumours are medulloblastomas?
questions.question: What percentage of childhood brain tumours are medulloblastomas?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 5% understates medulloblastoma's share; it is the most common malignant paediatric brain tumour and accounts for a substantially larger fraction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 10% also understates medulloblastoma's true share of childhood brain tumours.
explanations.C: Correct. Medulloblastoma accounts for approximately 20% of childhood brain tumours, making it the most common malignant (though not the single most common overall, a distinction held by the benign pilocytic astrocytoma) paediatric brain tumour. It also accounts for roughly 40% of paediatric posterior fossa tumours.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 40% overstates medulloblastoma's share of all childhood brain tumours, though it approximates its share of paediatric posterior fossa tumours specifically.

questions.learning_objective: State that medulloblastoma accounts for approximately 20% of childhood brain tumours.

questions.title: The VHL tumour suppressor gene is inactivated in which cerebellar tumour?
questions.question: The VHL tumour suppressor gene is inactivated in which of the following cerebellar tumours?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Medulloblastoma's characteristic genetic finding is isochromosome 17q (and, in a minority, germline APC or PTCH1 mutations), not VHL inactivation.
explanations.B: Correct. The VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3p is inactivated in hemangioblastoma, whether sporadic or as part of von Hippel-Lindau disease; loss of VHL stabilises hypoxia-inducible factors, driving the tumour's characteristic high vascularity via VEGF upregulation. Patients with multiple or recurrent hemangioblastomas should be screened for von Hippel-Lindau disease and its other manifestations.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pilocytic astrocytoma is characteristically driven by BRAF alterations (commonly a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion), not VHL inactivation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ependymoma is not characteristically driven by VHL inactivation; posterior fossa ependymomas are instead classified by molecular groups such as PFA and PFB.

questions.learning_objective: State that the VHL tumour suppressor gene is inactivated in hemangioblastoma.

questions.title: Which of the following is NOT a recognised morphological variant of medulloblastoma?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised morphological variant of medulloblastoma?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e., this IS a recognised variant). Classic medulloblastoma is the most common histological variant.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e., this IS a recognised variant). Desmoplastic/nodular medulloblastoma is a recognised variant, enriched for the SHH molecular subtype.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e., this IS a recognised variant). Large cell/anaplastic medulloblastoma is a recognised, generally higher-risk variant.
explanations.D: Correct. "Clear cell" is not a recognised morphological variant of medulloblastoma (the WHO-recognised variants are classic, desmoplastic/nodular, extensive nodularity, and large cell/anaplastic); clear-cell morphology in a cerebellar tumour instead raises other differentials such as clear cell ependymoma or metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Recognising which morphologies belong to the variant list, and which do not, avoids misclassifying an unrelated tumour as medulloblastoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that clear cell is not a recognised morphological variant of medulloblastoma.

questions.title: The WHO integrated diagnosis of medulloblastoma now requires which features?
questions.question: In medulloblastoma, the WHO classification now requires an integrated diagnosis that includes:

options.D: The patient's age and tumour location

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histological grade/variant alone was the older approach; the current WHO integrated diagnosis requires more than histology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Molecular subtype alone is also insufficient on its own for the current WHO integrated diagnosis; it is reported alongside, not instead of, histology.
explanations.C: Correct. Since the WHO 2016/2021 CNS tumour classification updates, the integrated diagnosis of medulloblastoma combines the traditional histological variant with the molecular subtype (WNT-activated, SHH-activated, Group 3 or Group 4), because together they better reflect underlying biology and prognosis. This dual reporting also guides risk stratification and, increasingly, treatment intensity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Patient age and tumour location are clinically relevant but are not the defining components of the WHO integrated pathological diagnosis, which is based on histopathology and molecular/genetic features.

questions.learning_objective: State that the WHO integrated diagnosis of medulloblastoma requires both histopathologic and molecular/genetic features.

questions.title: What is the clinical significance of medulloblastoma's radiosensitivity?
questions.question: Medulloblastoma is a highly malignant but radiosensitive tumour. What is the significance of its radiosensitivity?

options.A: It makes the tumour resistant to all forms of therapy.
options.B: It makes the tumour responsive to radiation therapy, which is a key part of treatment.
options.C: It means the tumour will spontaneously regress.
options.D: It means the tumour is only treatable with surgery.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Radiosensitivity means the opposite of therapy resistance — the tumour's cells are efficiently killed by ionising radiation.
explanations.B: Correct. Because medulloblastoma is markedly radiosensitive despite being a highly malignant, WHO Grade IV tumour, craniospinal radiotherapy (covering both the primary site and the neuroaxis, given its propensity for CSF-borne dissemination) is a cornerstone of adjuvant treatment after maximal safe surgical resection. Chemotherapy is also added in appropriate risk groups, particularly in young children in whom radiotherapy is minimised or delayed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Radiosensitivity describes response to radiotherapy, not a tendency toward spontaneous regression without treatment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Surgery alone is not curative for medulloblastoma; radiosensitivity is precisely why adjuvant radiotherapy (and chemotherapy in appropriate risk groups) is added after surgical resection.

questions.learning_objective: State that medulloblastoma's radiosensitivity makes radiotherapy a key part of its treatment, despite its high WHO grade.
